title: Safe Programming, Risk Triggers and Risk Categories
summary: Learn what safe programming means, how it applies across all your work, what a safeguarding risk and a trigger are, and the main risk categories with examples.

p: Safe programming does not mean removing all risk. It means making sure our work does not create or enable harm.
• Safe by design: make every programme, campaign and response safe for the people it reaches.
• No SEAH: programmes must not put children or adults at risk, especially women and girls, of sexual exploitation, abuse or harassment.
• Reduce wider harm: reduce the risk of gender-based violence, trafficking, modern slavery and all abuse within or because of our work.
• Protective environments: strengthen the places where our programmes happen.
• Do No Harm: the most basic principle of ethical programming.
Remember: some risk cannot be avoided. Safe programming is not the same as child protection programming. It cuts across all your work and functions.

b: Design and proposal: think about what the design could create (partners, people, setting, activities) and cost the safeguards.
Start-up: vet staff, volunteers and partners, brief everyone and set up reporting channels before meeting a single child.
Implementation: assess risk before every activity.
Monitoring: ask participants if they feel safe, check the register and update the risk assessment.
Close-out: safe exit for children and families, records stored or destroyed properly and lessons captured.

sections.h: Safe programming across all your work
p: Apply the same thinking to each type of activity.
• Case management: confidential records, safe interviews, informed consent and survivor-centred handling.
• Community outreach: who approves the visit, who goes, how the community knows how to report.
• Home visits: never alone with a child. Visits are planned, logged and supervised.
• Work with child domestic workers: never rely on the employer as the only route to the child. Plan for retaliation.
• Transport: vetted drivers, headcounts, no child alone with a driver, consent for travel.
• Residential activities: separate sleeping by age and gender, supervision rotas and night safety.
• Online engagement: approved platforms only, no private messaging with children and protected data.
• Partners and vendors: safeguarding clauses, briefings and monitoring for anyone with access.

img.cap: Plan safeguards together before any activity.

b: Who is at risk?
Who could cause harm?
What could go wrong?
What will we do to stop it, and who is responsible?

sections.h: What is a safeguarding risk, and what triggers it?
p: A safeguarding risk is anything in our work, our people or our environment that could lead to a child or adult being harmed, abused or exploited. A trigger is the situation that sets that risk in motion.
Common triggers:
• One-to-one contact with a child or adult at risk.
• Overnight or residential activities.
• Travel and transport.
• Home visits and outreach.
• Giving out cash, goods or stipends.
• New staff or volunteers brought in quickly.
• Events with photos, filming or media.
• Online platforms and group chats.
• Partners or vendors with direct access.
• Crises such as displacement, price shocks and insecurity.
• Large crowds and unclear supervision.
• Dependence: food, pay or shelter controlled by one person.

b: A risk is the harm that could happen. A trigger is what makes it more likely.
Your plan should deal with the trigger, not only the risk.

sections.h: Risk categories, with one example each
p: Use these categories to make sure you think widely.

• Context and environment: staff or representatives sexually exploit children or adults in the community. Risk factors: norms that accept exchange of money or gifts for sex, high poverty, many children out of school or in domestic work.

• Programme design and implementation: safeguarding is not built into the project, so no capacity or budget exists to prevent or respond. Risk factor: safeguarding left out of the proposal, budget and workplan from the start.
• Partnerships: a partner fails to detect, report or respond to a concern. Risk factors: no reporting system, low commitment from management, no monitoring.
• People: unsuitable people gain access to children. Risk factors: rushed recruitment, no reference checks, volunteers not vetted or supervised.
• Media and communications: a child's identity and location are revealed through a photo or story. Risk factors: no informed consent, name, image and location combined, no sign-off.
• Digital and information: a child is groomed through a programme WhatsApp group or social media. Risk factors: staff unaware of online risks, personal numbers shared, no platform rules.
• Supply chain: an unchecked driver or vendor harms a child. Risk factors: no safeguarding clause in the contract, no briefing, no supervision.

b: Choose one activity.
For each of the seven categories, write one risk that could apply.
Star the two most serious.

activity: Choose one real activity in your organisation. List at least one risk for each of the seven categories and the trigger behind each one. Circle the two most serious risks.

The score given to a risk on a chart

title: Risk Assessment: Types, Procedure, Scoring and Escalation
summary: Learn the four types of risk assessment, follow the six-step procedure, score risks with the impact and likelihood grid, and know when and how to escalate.

sections.h: Four types of safeguarding risk assessment
p: Use the right type at the right time.

• Proposal or programme design: done at design stage. It is not a deep analysis. Think through what risks the design could create from partners, people, setting and activities, and cost the safeguards into the budget. When: before submitting a proposal.
• Organisational: an organisation-wide look at risks across all functions: HR, finance, procurement, communications, programmes and IT. When: yearly, and when things change.
• Project: all the safeguarding risks for one project over its life, with owners and actions, tracked over time. When: at start-up and reviewed every quarter.
• Activity-level: a specific activity or event, such as a school talk, a home visit, a camp or a training. Often a checklist plus a short risk table. When: before every activity.

b: A new proposal to a donor: proposal assessment.
A yearly review of all functions: organisational assessment.
A one-day outreach in a community: activity-level assessment.

sections.h: The risk assessment procedure, step by step
p: Follow six steps.
• 1. Identify the risk. What could go wrong? Ask 'can it happen?', not only 'will it happen?'. Use your categories and triggers.
• 2. Who is at risk? Children, adults at risk, staff, community members. Be specific.
• 3. Rate impact and likelihood, then work out the score and level.
• 4. Plan actions to reduce the risk. Deal with the triggers, not only the risk.
• 5. Name an owner and a date for every action, and the resources needed.
• 6. Review. Before the activity and regularly after. Yesterday's risk is not today's risk.

b: Activity | Identified risk | Who is at risk | Impact | Likelihood | Score and level | Action to reduce the risk | Who is responsible | When due | Resources needed | Last reviewed.

p: Score = (Impact x Likelihood) + Impact. Impact counts twice, so serious harm matters even when it is unlikely.
Impact scale: Negligible (1), Moderate (2), Significant (3), Severe (4), Extreme (5).
Likelihood scale: Rare (1), Unlikely (2), Possible (3), Likely (4), Near certain (5).
Worked examples:
• Severe impact (4) and possible likelihood (3): (4 x 3) + 4 = 16, which is High.
• Extreme impact (5) and rare likelihood (1): (5 x 1) + 5 = 10, which is Medium.
• Significant impact (3) and likely (4): (3 x 4) + 3 = 15, which is High.
• Negligible impact (1) and rare (1): (1 x 1) + 1 = 2, which is Very low.
Risk levels:
• E, Extreme (22 and above): stop or redesign the activity and escalate now.
• H, High (15 to 21): do not proceed without strong action and management approval.
• M, Medium (10 to 14): reduce the risk, assign owners and monitor closely.
• L, Low (5 to 9): manage with routine controls.
• VL, Very low (2 to 4): note and review.

b: Impact 5, likelihood 3: score (5 x 3) + 5 = 20, High.
Impact 4, likelihood 5: score (4 x 5) + 4 = 24, Extreme.
Impact 2, likelihood 3: score (2 x 3) + 2 = 8, Low.

sections.h: A worked example of a risk row
p: Here is one filled row as a model.
• Activity: home visit to a child domestic worker.
• Identified risk: a staff member alone with the child in the employer's house.
• Who is at risk: the child and the staff member.
• Impact: Severe (4). Likelihood: Possible (3). Score and level: 16, High.
• Action to reduce the risk: visits in pairs, meet the child in a visible space, debrief afterwards.
• Who is responsible: programme lead. When due: from the next visit.
• Resources: transport for two staff. Last reviewed: noted with the date.
Good habits:
• Make each row specific to the activity, not generic.
• Make every action realistic, owned and dated.
• Ask others: what risk is missing?

ex.t: Activity: run a full risk assessment on a real activity
b: Choose one real activity, ideally one that reaches children at risk.
Start from your power map and risk list. Add risks for every category and trigger that applies.
Fill in at least five risks with who is at risk, impact, likelihood, action, owner and due date.
Flag anything High or Extreme and write how you would escalate it.
Swap with another team and review: are risks specific, are actions realistic, what is missing?

sections.h: Escalating risk: when, how and to whom
p: Some risks cannot be handled at your level.
When to escalate:
• The risk is High or Extreme.
• You cannot reduce it with the resources you have.
• An incident or near-miss happens.
• The setting changes: a new site, a crisis or a new partner.
How:
• In writing, not just a hallway conversation.
• Update the risk register with the new score.
• Propose a decision: reduce, redesign, pause or stop.
• Record the decision and who made it.
To whom:
• Activity lead to the SFP/DSL.
• SFP/DSL to management or the executive director.
• Executive director to the board for extreme risks.
• To donors where your agreement requires it.
Some risks that are very likely and very serious need you to stop the activity. Pausing to rethink costs less than harm or damage.

ex.t: Ten things to know about risk assessments (1 to 5)
b: 1 Risk assessment is a form of care: think ahead about what could go wrong.
2 Likelihood is not impact: rare events can be fatal.
3 Ask 'can it happen?', not only 'will it happen?'.
4 Some risks mean stopping.
5 Not all risks are obvious: ask participants and stakeholders.

title: Safer Spaces, Safe Partnerships and Risk Assessment in Practice
summary: Set up safer spaces, build safe partnerships, learn ten practitioner tips for risk assessment, and run risk assessment workshops with your team.

p: A safer space is a place where children and adults can take part without fear.
• Venues are visible and well lit, with safe toilets separated by gender.
• No hidden rooms, and no locked door with a child inside.
• Supervision ratios are set for every activity.
• Visitors sign in, are identified and are never left alone with children.
• Children and staff can be identified (name tags or T-shirts).
• Children are asked where they feel safe and unsafe.

b: Walk around the venue before the activity.
Look for blind spots, unlocked gates, unsafe toilets and unclear exits.
Fix what you can and note what you cannot.

p: Partners and vendors can reach children through your programme. They must meet the same standard.
• Assess a partner's safeguarding before you sign.
• Put safeguarding clauses and your code of conduct in every agreement.
• Include safeguarding time in every kick-off meeting.
• Agree clear reporting lines between you and the partner.
• Monitor, support and review the partner's practice.
• Apply the same expectations to vendors with access to programme sites.

b: Do you have a safeguarding policy and a named lead?
How do you check staff and volunteers?
How do people report concerns to you?
Will you sign our code of conduct?

sections.h: Practitioner's notes: ten things to know (6 to 10 and a recap)
p: Keep these in mind.
• 6. Everyone helps identify risks, not just the safeguarding team.
• 7. Mind the triggers. Your plan should address what sets a risk in motion.
• 8. Incomplete action is an incomplete process. Plans that are not monitored make the assessment meaningless.
• 9. Yesterday's risk is not today's risk. 'We did it last year' is not enough. Update regularly.
• 10. You are probably already assessing risk. You just need to write it down. Documentation is the difference between good intention and compliance.
Recap of 1 to 5: risk assessment is care; likelihood is not impact; ask 'can it happen?'; some risks mean stopping; not all risks are obvious.

b: It is often a skills problem, not a willingness problem.
People skip risk assessments when no one has shown them how.

p: A short workshop builds skill and gets the assessment done at the same time.
• Bring the project team together for one to two hours: programme, MEAL, logistics and community staff.
• Explain the categories and triggers with one worked example.
• Use the risk prompts to brainstorm risks for each category.
• Score and plan actions together, and give owners in the room.
• Agree the review date and put it in the calendar before people leave.

img.alt: A trainer writing steps on a flip chart in front of a group
img.cap: A short workshop can build skills and produce a finished assessment.

b: A checklist attached to every activity request, signed by a named person and approved by the programme lead.
It covers health and safety, basic needs, activity design, information and accountability and travel.
A short risk table: risk area, rating, controls, likelihood, prevention, owner and deadline.
Completed forms are filed by quarter so they can be checked later.

title: Safer Recruitment and Induction
summary: Learn why safer recruitment matters and the steps before and after employment: adverts, interviews, references, checks, conditional offers, induction, supervision and exit.

sections.h: What safer recruitment is, and why we do it
p: Safer recruitment is how we block access to people who could harm children or adults at risk, and make sure everyone we bring in is fit to work with children and shares our values. It is one of the strongest forms of prevention we have.
• Block access: people who want to harm children look for organisations with weak checks.
• Fit for children: skills are not enough. Conduct and attitude matter.
• Value fit: people who already believe in dignity and safety are easier to keep safe.
Example safeguarding statement for adverts and job descriptions:

• '[Organisation] is committed to safeguarding children and adults at risk, and expects everyone who works with us to share this commitment. The successful candidate will go through safer recruitment checks, including references and background checks, and must sign our Safeguarding Policy and Code of Conduct.'

b: Why is safer recruitment important? List as many answers as you can in two minutes.

p: Use these steps from advert to offer.
• Advert and job description: a safeguarding statement in every advert, and safeguarding duties in the job description.
• Application form: ask about gaps in employment and why the person left previous roles. Include one safeguarding question.
• Share your policy early: send the policy and code of conduct before the interview so candidates know what you expect.
• Values-based interview: at least one safeguarding question, and a panel member who understands safeguarding.
• Self-declaration: the candidate declares any past allegations, investigations or convictions.
• Reference checks: at least two, including the last employer. Ask directly about conduct with children or adults at risk.
• Background and identity checks: confirm ID and address, check certificates, use guarantors and screen social media.
• Police report and affidavit: a police character report where available and a sworn affidavit of good conduct.
• Role-specific checks: driving test and licence check for drivers, and health checks where the role needs them.
• Misconduct Disclosure Scheme: an inter-agency scheme in which employers share past sexual misconduct findings when asked for references.
• Conditional offer: the offer becomes final only when all checks are back and clear.
• Record it: keep a checks tracker for every hire so it can be audited.

img.alt: Women sitting around a table in an interview or meeting
img.cap: A good interview panel includes someone who understands safeguarding.

ex.t: A checks tracker (a model, with no names)
b: Columns: staff member | referee check | guarantor check | social media screening | ID and address verification | status.
Each person has a row, with 'completed' or 'cleared' filled in as checks come back.
The tracker is checked by HR and the SFP/DSL.

p: Safety continues after the person starts.
• Sign-off: the policy and code of conduct are signed on day one.
• Induction within 30 days, and before unsupervised contact with children.
• Probation with a safeguarding review before confirmation.
• Supervision and appraisal: one safeguarding objective in every plan.
• Refreshers every year, plus briefings when risks change.
• Re-checks when someone moves into a role with more access.
• Exit: exit interviews, and honest references that include proven misconduct.

ex.t: Activity: draft three values-based interview questions
b: Pick a role your organisation often hires for, such as field officer, teacher, driver or volunteer.
Write three questions that begin 'Tell me about a time...' or 'What would you do if...'.
For each, write what a good answer shows and the red flags to listen for.
Example: 'What would you do if a child asked you to keep a secret?' A good answer: listen, explain you cannot promise secrecy and tell the safeguarding lead. A red flag: 'I would keep it between us.'

p: Avoid these.
• Rushing a hire and doing checks later, or never.
• Asking only about skills and ignoring conduct.
• Accepting a reference from a friend of the candidate instead of the last employer.
• Letting a volunteer start work with children before induction.
• Giving a 'good' reference to push out a person with proven misconduct.
• No record of checks, so nothing can be audited.
What to do instead:
• Make safeguarding checks a rule for everyone, including senior staff, volunteers and drivers.
• Keep a checks tracker for each role and review it every quarter.

b: Do all job adverts include the safeguarding statement?
Do we ask for two references and speak to the last employer?
Does anyone work with children before induction?
